newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Di Pietro quits as minister over probe.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Di Pietro quits as minister over probe.

text.p: The star of Italy's assault on graft, former magistrate Antonio Di Pietro, resigned from the government on Thursday after coming under investigation himself.
In a bitter letter to Prime Minister Romano Prodi, he said he had become the victim of a "pigeon shoot" and announced he was quitting his cabinet post as public works minister.
His move followed confirmation from his lawyer Massimo Dinoia that he was the subject of a preliminary investigation by magistrates in the northern town of Brescia.
The shock decision made Di Pietro, a non-partisan appointee and one of the most popular figures in Italy, the first minister to resign from Prodi's six-month-old centre-left cabinet.
It was not immediately clear whether his resignation had been accepted.
Several ministers rushed to limit the potential damage, saying the move would have no effect on government stability.
"I really do not think so. But it is up to Prime Minister Prodi to express his own view," Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini told Reuters when asked whether it would have an impact.

Di Pietro was the star investigator of the elite pool of "Clean Hands" magistrates in Milan that exposed deep corruption in politics and brought down the country's post-war governing class with its bombshell investigations.

He quit as a magistrate in December 1994 shortly after the Milan team placed then conservative prime minister Silvio Berlusconi under investigation for alleged bribery but has never fully explained why he resigned.
Newspapers on Thursday said Di Pietro was being probed over alleged irregularities in the way he conducted his inquiries.
"Enough is enough," D Pietro wrote in his letter of resignation, which said the decision was irreversible.
He said he had learned of the inquiry from television.
"For years now I have been subjected to investigations and enquiries of all kinds, legal and illegal, and always unjustly," Di Pietro wrote.

"Even so, the pigeon shoot goes on because they are trying to make me pay at any cost for the only thing they can pin on me, and of which I'm proud, and that is that I wanted to do my duty," he wrote.
The reference was to a string of past investigations against Di Pietro which he and supporters have portrayed as a vendetta by players in the Tangentopoli (Bribesville) scandal he exposed.

He was the target of an earlier probe by Brescia magistrates into allegations of corruption and of profiting from holding a public office. All charges against him were dropped in April shortly before Prodi named him to his cabinet.
Reaction from media mogul Berlusconi's centre-right Freedom Alliance to Di Pietro's resignation was wry and ironic.

Former justice minister Filippo Mancuso, who was ousted from his post last year in a no-confidence vote over attempts to rein in the Milan magistrates, said he was certain Di Pietro had "reasons to resign".
"I hope, if the reason is a judicial one, that he finds judges who are totally different from him," Mancuso said.

Another conservative politician called the move a typical act of drama from Di Pietro, who had Italians rivetted to their television screens during live broadcasts of one of the biggest corruption trials he prosecuted in 1993 and 1994.
"Just two weeks ago he said he was preparing to throw off his ministry in exactly the same way he threw off his robes," she said.
